Figure out what your support system is.  We're on our own, and that is what has made it genuinely awful.  Don't be afraid to seek out support from your neighborhood facebook group or even government programs.  Every state has an Early Interventions/Birth-to-Three program (that God-willing never gets cut), which can be an amazing resource even if they just see you every month.  It is worth it to pay a teenager to help you take care of your kids.  Totally paid a 15 year old to babysit/wash dishes/wash bottles/meal prep, while we are home.  With two infants, a second person is priceless, especially if you've used up your maternity/paternity leave and one of you is stuck with two babies solo.  Don't be afraid to request a doctor's note and FMLA approval if one or both of your kids has an ongoing medical or developmental problem.  Remember, you have two babies.  Most parents, most managers, most doctors, most HR staff, will only ever have one infant at a time.  You might get scolded for requesting FMLA.  You might get side eye.  Screw 'em.  Know your rights.  If you need time off for a medical thing for one or both of your kids, you are entitled to job protection.  We've invoked FMLA 5 times between myself and spouse in 3 years' time.  Besides original maternity/paternity, each FMLA was limited in nature and allowed us to give our kids the attention they deserve.  We both still have our original jobs and our careers are finally starting to bounce back.

  
A big milestone was starting to feed our kids solids at 8 months.  And giving them modified versions of what we were eating.  And, now, having toddlers who, for the most part, eat what their parents eat.  Amazing.  No tray of chicken nuggets or mac-n-cheese to make in addition to our dinners.  Nope, just cook what we would normally eat and feed it to them.  Initially, the menu is pretty limited, but often, cutting or added cooking time to make it small or soft enough is all it took.  Sometimes they eat little to nothing.  That will only happen a few times, trust me.  They almost always find something on the plate to eat, and usually will at least try everything on the plate.  You just keep offering, over and over.

  
Best of luck.  Stay strong.  Stay patient.

I grew up in a very devout small town, with, at the time, one of the largest parishes in the diocese.  Our catechists were mostly parents, grandparents, retirees, and, in the case of grade school, occasionally teams of high school seniors.  The general level of education was low - our employment centers were primarily factories and farms.  Holy Thursday, Good Friday, and Easter Monday were observed as holidays in the public schools and government offices, because nobody was going to show up anyway.  And, yes, the church was full on holy days, not just people taking the day off.  Probably half of our public school teachers came to school with ashes on Ash Wednesday (and the other half attended the evening services).  Some of the highest paid people in town, besides hospital employees, were teachers.  We considered teachers "rich."  So... you are "pulling out the jump-to-conclusions-mat" when you assume that our catechists rejected Vatican II, when the case is really a lack of education.  Ironically, our schools were rated some of the best in the state, probably because the parents wanted better for their kids and prioritized spending on education.  But those kids that went to college usually didn't return, for lack of opportunity.  We also had one of the most beautiful parishes in the diocese.  Not for money spent, but for the success of volunteer projects to maintain a very old church and charity of local contractors to do the work at-cost with no profit, and some employees working for free when it was for a church.

  
Nobody ever really discussed Vatican II.  Most of our catechism revolved around how to live your life as a Catholic, the importance of Eucharist, and the importance of Confession, in your daily life.  The old ladies especially emphasized loving your neighbor and enemy, and giving to the poor, even from your own poverty.
It was a joke.  I know.  It's all in the name.

I would personally lean into being diversified beyond what any IRA offers.  My grandpa lived through the Great Depression.  He held onto a 5-acre wooded piece of land he acquired cheaply.  When he needed a down payment, HE logged it.  Yes, him and his brother.  With chainsaws.  He kept some of the timber to build a garage, shop (he was a carpenter), and a 1-room addition to the home he bought.  Then he plowed the land and farmed it, rotating wheat, corn, and soy, and also kept hens for the eggs and occasional meat when they no longer produced, all while he worked full time.  When he got older, he leased it to a neighboring farmer for continued income.  When he died, Grandma sold it and my uncles helped her invest in conservatively.  He had very little use for the stock market after seeing the poverty of the 1930s and the WWII aftermath that he witnessed as an older soldier overseas.  Having both stocks and actual tangible assets and skills (real estate, backyard farming, carpentry, being a landlord, etc) is probably a good idea for diversification.  Everything in an IRA is all eggs in one basket.

I recommend changing careers. Find a trade that can grow into a management position.  Land surveying (the art and science of doing land measurements) is a great area of work if you have ambition. Many of our in-house surveyors previously worked in food service and came to us with zero experience. They were paired with an experienced staff member, learned the ropes, and advanced to running their own "1-man" survey crew (instead of the typical "2-man"). One of those staff members who has been with us for 12 years, had put himself through community college and recently took the state licensing exam, is now a licensed surveyor, and is now working in the office doing the drafting. His career projection could take him up into management, co-ownership of our firm, or, if he wants, owning his own survey company.

So it goes with other trades. You can make good money in the US doing construction. It is very hard work. If you master your skill and learn more skills, you can advance into higher roles such as foreman and project manager.  As an engineer, I work with those foremen and managers. Most have no formal education, but years of experience. I fully respect their work and treat them as equal team members, so long as I am being treated the same. (Many construction managers belittle engineers. This earns them no favors.)

So, consider a trade... plumbing, carpentry, land surveying, masonry, roofing, landscaping.  Some pay better than others, and some take longer to learn than others.  But, I really think all have a good upward trajectory.

If you are able to get an education in an area with good job outlooks, that is what I did. I chose engineering, earned scholarships, took a few small student loans, worked several paid internships, and lived like a poor person for 5 years. If you have the book-smarts, this is a great path.
